strengths: MMEarth-Bench is a substantial and carefully engineered contribution: five new tasks (biomass, three soil properties, species occurrence) with 12 aligned modalities per task, globally distributed samples, and both random and geographic (Africa held-out) test splits. This fills a real gap relative to existing EO benchmarks that typically offer only 1-3 modalities and regional coverage.

The dataset construction pipeline is documented in extensive and reproducible detail in the supplementary (GEDI/WoSIS/IUCN sourcing, quality filtering, cloud filtering for Sentinel-2, tile generation, overlap removal, normalization statistics), which supports reproducibility and appropriate data attribution.

Benchmarking is thorough: 7 diverse pretrained models (RGB-only, S2-only, multimodal) plus a randomly initialized baseline, evaluated across three training-data regimes (5%/50%/100%), finetuning and linear probing, with three seeds and statistical testing (Wilcoxon with Holm-Bonferroni correction), yielding credible and nuanced findings (e.g., multimodal pretraining helps but geographic generalization remains poor; multimodal finetuning can sometimes hurt OOD generalization).

TTT-MMR is a simple, model-agnostic idea (using all test-time modalities as reconstruction targets via a frozen decoder, with per-modality gradient normalization) that is architecture-independent and applicable beyond the benchmark itself (practitioner's guide provided). The geographic-batching variant (TTT-MMR-GEO) offers an intuitive and effective trade-off between specialization and regularization.

Results consistently show improvement of TTT-MMR/TTT-MMR-GEO over the JT baseline across all 8 models, 5 tasks, and both splits, with supporting statistical significance and multiple metrics (raw delta and relative improvement) provided in the supplementary for robustness.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison for the TTT method is essentially limited to a single baseline (joint training, JT). Despite extensively discussing TENT, S4T, UDA-SS, and other TTA/UDA methods in Related Work, none are run as quantitative baselines, making it hard to judge how much of the improvement is attributable to the specific multimodal-reconstruction design versus generic test-time adaptation with batching/regularization.

The "geographic" generalization evaluation reduces to a single held-out continent (Africa) versus "rest of world"; while a reasonable and practically motivated choice, this is only one axis of geographic shift and the paper's broader claims about "geographic generalization" and models' ability to generalize globally rest on this one split.

Despite the framing as global and covering "nature," the species task is restricted to 100 terrestrial mammal species (chosen via somewhat ad hoc area-threshold filtering) and the modality set, while broad (12), is fixed to those in MMEarth pretraining data, meaning the benchmark's coverage of modality diversity and species/task diversity is narrower than the framing might suggest.

Absolute performance after TTT remains weak or even strongly negative in several settings (e.g., soil organic carbon geographic R2 remains largely negative even after adaptation), so while relative/statistical improvements are demonstrated, the practical impact on downstream task usability in the hardest OOD settings is limited.

Some methodological choices (batch size 8, learning rate 1e-2, max 5 TTT iterations, gradient normalization scheme) are fixed without extensive ablation or sensitivity analysis in the main text, leaving open how sensitive the method is to these hyperparameters across different tasks/architectures.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful benchmark (MMEarth-Bench) with five new global tasks sharing 12 aligned modalities (imagery, map products, climate variables), addressing a real gap identified via a thorough comparison table against six prior EO benchmarks (Copernicus-Bench, PANGAEA, PhilEO, FoMo-Bench, GEO-Bench, SustainBench).

Careful and well-documented dataset construction pipeline (GEDI biomass sampling balanced across biomes/ecoregions, WoSIS soil filtering, IUCN species range sampling with explicit in/out-of-Africa area thresholds), with extensive supplementary detail supporting reproducibility (H5 file formats, GeoJSON schemas, no-data value tables, per-split statistics, missing-modality counts).

Deliberate geographic held-out test split (Africa) in addition to random split, directly targeting the underexplored problem of geographic generalization, which is a meaningful and timely contribution to the EO/geospatial ML community.

Benchmarks a genuinely diverse set of 7 pretrained models (RGB-only, S2-only, and multimodal; CNN, ViT, Swin architectures) plus a randomly initialized baseline, both with finetuning and linear probing, yielding informative findings (e.g., persistent geographic generalization gap, multimodal input sometimes hurting OOD finetuning performance).

The proposed TTT-MMR method is simple, model-agnostic, and architecture-agnostic (works with transformers lacking batch norm, unlike TENT), and is well-motivated relative to related TTA/UDA/JT literature.

Strong empirical validation of the method: consistent improvements across all 8 models, all 5 tasks, and both test splits, with statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon with Holm-Bonferroni correction), three random seeds, and both raw-delta and relative-improvement metrics reported for robustness.

Extensive supplementary material (raw per-seed results, linear probing comparisons, modality reconstruction visualizations, compute-time analysis, practitioner's guide) substantially strengthens transparency and usability for the community.
weaknesses: The geographic OOD evaluation relies on a single held-out continent (Africa); while well-motivated by data scarcity concerns, this limits the generality of claims about 'geographic generalization' and leaves open whether findings transfer to other continental shifts (e.g., held-out Oceania or South America).

Some geographic test splits are quite small (soil tasks have only 232-349 tiles in the geographic split), which may lead to noisy R2 estimates, as reflected in large negative R2 values and wide error bars in several figures.

The species task selection (top 100 species by list order after filtering) is a somewhat ad hoc procedure that could introduce taxonomic bias (Fig. S.4 shows heavy skew toward Chiroptera/Rodentia), potentially limiting how representative this task is of broader species distribution modeling.

The technical novelty of TTT-MMR is incremental relative to prior JT/TTT and multimodal TTA literature (Sec. 2), largely combining existing ideas (joint training, per-modality gradient normalization, geographic batching) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the contribution is more in careful empirical validation than algorithmic innovation.

Absolute performance gains from TTT-MMR are often modest (e.g., median deltas frequently below 0.05 R2/mAP in Fig. 7), and for some models/tasks (e.g., Copernicus-FM, TerraMind) the relative improvement is quite small (Table S.10), raising the question of practical significance in some settings even though statistical significance is established.

No direct quantitative comparison to alternative TTA baselines beyond JT (e.g., adapting TENT-style entropy or other generic TTA baselines to the regression setting) is provided, which would help contextualize the magnitude of improvement against other simple adaptation strategies.

strengths: Introduces a substantial new multimodal Earth observation benchmark (MMEarth-Bench) with 12 aligned modalities across 5 globally distributed environmental tasks (biomass, three soil properties, species occurrence), filling a clear gap in existing EO benchmarks that typically have few modalities and/or non-global, non-geographic-split data.

Very thorough experimental evaluation: 8 diverse pretrained models (RGB/S2/multimodal) plus randomly initialized baselines, evaluated under finetuning and linear probing, at three training-data fractions, on both random and geographic (held-out Africa) test splits — yielding useful, non-trivial findings (e.g., multimodal-from-scratch models are competitive with pretrained ones given enough data; persistent geographic generalization gap across nearly all models/tasks).

Proposes TTT-MMR, a model-agnostic test-time training method that repurposes all available (not just input-compatible) modalities as reconstruction targets, with a principled per-modality gradient normalization scheme; demonstrates consistent, statistically significant improvements (Wilcoxon with Holm-Bonferroni correction) across all 10 models, 5 tasks, and both test splits.

The geographic-batching variant (TTT-MMR-Geo) is shown to meaningfully improve performance on long-tail/rare samples, a practically important and intuitively well-explained result (tiles nearby are more likely similar, giving less diluted gradients).

Excellent supplementary materials: detailed and reproducible dataset generation pipeline, practitioner's guide for applying the method to new tasks, compute-cost analysis showing the method is lightweight (<1 sec/sample), an interactive data explorer, extensive ablations (modality leave-one-out, iteration counts, reconstruction quality before/after TTT), and full raw results tables across seeds.

Careful attention to evaluation methodology, including both R² and mAP metrics, relative improvement normalization for cross-task comparison, and multiple random seeds with standard errors reported throughout.
weaknesses: The core TTT-MMR method is a fairly incremental combination of established ideas (joint training with auxiliary reconstruction heads, test-time training via self-supervised losses, batching for regularization); its novelty lies mainly in using many modalities jointly and per-modality gradient normalization rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Reported performance gains from TTT are statistically significant but often numerically modest (small R² deltas in Fig. 7), and some models/tasks show negligible or slightly negative relative improvement on certain splits (e.g., Galileo and ConvNeXtV2A-MM on the random split per Table A.15), somewhat tempering the practical impact claims.

The geographic generalization analysis relies on a single held-out continent (Africa) as the sole geographic distribution shift; while well-motivated, this limits the generality of conclusions about "geographic generalization" and it is unclear how findings would transfer to other continents or shift types.

Some causal explanations for observed phenomena (e.g., multimodal finetuning overfitting to non-Africa domain, erasure of pretrained regional information) are plausible but speculative, without additional targeted experiments to confirm the proposed mechanisms.
The benchmark's soil datasets carry a CC BY-NC license and the species dataset uses IUCN terms of use, which may constrain broader (e.g., commercial) reuse compared to fully open benchmarks.

Dataset construction pipeline is complex (multi-stage GEE queries, quality filters, ecoregion-based sampling), which, despite code release, may pose a nontrivial reproducibility/extension burden for other groups wanting to add new tasks or modalities.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated benchmark (MMEarth-Bench) that addresses a clear gap: existing EO benchmarks lack many co-registered modalities, global coverage, and explicit geographic held-out splits. Providing 12 aligned modalities across 5 tasks (biomass, three soil properties, species occurrence) with random and geographic test splits is a valuable community resource.

Extensive and carefully documented dataset construction pipeline (GEDI sampling stratified by biome/ecoregion, WoSIS soil filtering, IUCN species range sampling, cloud filtering for Sentinel-2, missing-modality handling), with thorough appendix documentation supporting reproducibility, plus a released interactive Explorer tool and downloadable H5/JSON formats.

Broad and fair benchmarking of 8 diverse pretrained models (RGB-only, S2-only, multimodal) plus randomly initialized baselines, across three training-data regimes (5%/50%/100%), with both finetuning and linear probing, and both random and geographic test splits — this yields genuinely informative findings (e.g., persistent geographic generalization gap, competitiveness of randomly initialized multimodal models with enough labels).

The proposed TTT-MMR method is simple, model-agnostic, and architecture-agnostic (works without batch norm, unlike TENT), and is shown empirically to improve performance across all 10 models, all 5 tasks, and both splits, with statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon + Holm-Bonferroni correction).

The geographic-batching variant (TTT-MMR-Geo) is a sensible, well-motivated regularization/specialization trade-off, and the long-tail analysis convincingly shows a distinct practical benefit (reduced underestimation for rare biomass/soil values and rare species) that random batching does not achieve.

Good ablations in the appendix (modality leave-one-out, iteration counts, inference-time cost, best-model-only TTT benefit, relative-improvement metric) that support robustness of the claims beyond the main text figures.
weaknesses: Many of the absolute TTT-MMR / TTT-MMR-Geo gains are quite small (e.g., median deltas often <0.02 R2 for several tasks/splits per Fig. 7), and some tasks/splits (e.g., soil OC geographic split) remain deeply negative R2 even after adaptation, tempering the practical significance of the proposed improvement despite statistical significance.

The TTT-MMR method requires a joint-training (JT) stage with a task modality decoder trained on all 12 modalities beforehand, which is a nontrivial training-time assumption; the paper could better clarify how sensitive results are to availability of all modalities at JT time versus only a subset, and how the method degrades if fewer target modalities are available at test time (a partial ablation exists in the appendix but is limited to one seed/model).

Cross-architecture comparisons (e.g., 'multimodal models outperform unimodal') are confounded by differing backbone sizes, pretraining datasets, and pretraining objectives; while the S2-only vs. multimodal same-model comparisons (TerraMind/Copernicus-FM/Galileo) help isolate the modality effect, the broader 8-model comparison conflates architecture/scale/data effects with modality-count effects.

The species task is built from only 100 preselected mammal species meeting an ad hoc area threshold in/out of Africa, and biomass/soil sampling choices (balancing by biome, restricting to shallow soil depth) may limit how representative the benchmark is of the broader diversity of EO downstream applications; this narrows the generality of conclusions somewhat.

The number of TTT iterations is tuned per-model/task using the validation set (mean of best iteration across validation batches), which adds a hyperparameter selection step not fully characterized in terms of computational overhead trade-offs beyond the reported per-sample inference time.

The paper combines a dataset contribution and a method contribution; while both are reasonably well done, neither receives the depth of investigation it might if presented alone (e.g., limited theoretical analysis of why per-modality gradient normalization stabilizes TTT, no comparison against alternative advanced TTA baselines like TENT variants adapted for regression or other multimodal TTA baselines from the related work discussion).
